grammar.title: Family words — my family vs. your family
grammar.pattern: 父 / 母 (my) ・ お父さん / お母さん (someone's)
grammar.meaning: Different words for your own family and for other people's families
grammar.explanation: Japanese has two sets of family words. When you talk about your own family to other people, use the plain, humble words: 父 (my father), 母 (my mother), 兄 (my older brother). When you talk about someone else's family, use the polite words, which often look like お〜さん: お父さん, お母さん, お兄さん. For younger siblings just add さん: 弟さん, 妹さん. Inside the family, you also call older relatives with the polite words — a child calls out お母さん to Mom.
notes: My family: 父 (ちち), 母 (はは), 兄 (あに), 姉 (あね), 弟 (おとうと), 妹 (いもうと), 両親 (りょうしん), 夫 (おっと), 妻 (つま), 息子 (むすこ), 娘 (むすめ).
Someone's family: お父さん, お母さん, お兄さん, お姉さん, 弟さん, 妹さん, ご両親 (ごりょうしん), 息子さん, 娘さん.
Japanese always says older or younger: there is no single word for just "brother" or "sister".

grammar.title: 〜人 — counting people
grammar.pattern: 一人・二人・三人… ／ 何人
grammar.meaning: one person, two people, three people… / how many people
grammar.explanation: To count people, add 人 to a number. The first two are special: 一人 is ひとり and 二人 is ふたり. From three on, 人 is read にん: 三人 (さんにん), 五人 (ごにん), 十人 (じゅうにん). Four people is よにん, not よんにん. To ask how many people, say 何人 (なんにん). To say you have family members, use います from Unit 7: 兄が一人います — I have one older brother.
notes: 一人 (ひとり), 二人 (ふたり), 三人 (さんにん), 四人 (よにん), 五人 (ごにん), 六人 (ろくにん), 七人 (ななにん / しちにん), 八人 (はちにん), 九人 (きゅうにん), 十人 (じゅうにん).
The number usually comes right before います: 子どもが二人います.
何人家族ですか = How many people are in your family? Answer: 四人家族です.

grammar.title: 〜ています — ongoing states (live, married, know)
grammar.pattern: 住んでいます ／ 結婚しています ／ 知っています
grammar.explanation: Some verbs describe a state that continues, not a one-time action. Japanese says these with a form ending in 〜ています. For now, learn three as set phrases: 住んでいます (live somewhere), 結婚しています (am married) and 知っています (know). The place where you live takes に: 東京に住んでいます. In Unit 9 you'll learn how to build this form from any verb.
notes: Negative: 住んでいません, 結婚していません — but "I don't know" is 知りません, not 知っていません.
Use に for the place you live: 大阪に住んでいます.
Use を for the person or thing you know: 田中さんを知っていますか.

grammar.title: 〜くて / 〜で — joining adjectives ("… and …")
grammar.explanation: To join two descriptions in one sentence, change the first adjective into its て-form. For い-adjectives, drop the final い and add くて: 明るい → 明るくて, 若い → 若くて. For な-adjectives, just add で: まじめ → まじめで, きれい → きれいで. Only the last adjective shows the tense and politeness, so 明るくて、きれいです means "is cheerful and pretty". いい is irregular: it becomes よくて.
notes: いい → よくて (irregular): 頭がいい → 頭がよくて.
Nouns work like な-adjectives: 兄は銀行員で、姉は看護師です (my brother is a bank employee, and my sister is a nurse).
Join two good things or two bad things. For good + bad, use が (but) instead.

grammar.title: もう / まだ — already, still, not yet
grammar.pattern: もう Vました ／ いいえ、まだです ／ まだ N です
grammar.explanation: もう means "already" and まだ means "still" or "not yet". Ask もう〜ましたか to find out if someone has already done something: もう昼ごはんを食べましたか. If you have, say はい、もう食べました; if you haven't yet, say いいえ、まだです. With nouns and adjectives, まだ means "still": 弟はまだ学生です — my brother is still a student. もう with a noun means "already": 娘はもう大人です.
notes: Don't answer "not yet" with 食べませんでした — that means "I didn't eat". Say まだです.
With the set phrase from this unit: まだ結婚していません = not married yet.
In Unit 9 you'll learn the full "not yet" form: まだ食べていません.

grammar.title: 〜が上手 / 下手 / 好き / きらい — skills and likes
grammar.pattern: A は B が 好き / きらい / 上手 / 下手 です
grammar.meaning: A likes / dislikes / is good at / is bad at B
grammar.explanation: With 好き (like), きらい (dislike), 上手 (good at) and 下手 (bad at), the thing you like or are good at is marked with が, not を. So "I like music" is 私は音楽が好きです. These four words are な-adjectives, so before a noun they take な: 好きなスポーツ (a sport I like). To ask what someone likes, say 何が好きですか. 上手 is a compliment for other people; about yourself it sounds like bragging, so people usually answer a compliment with いいえ、まだ下手です.
notes: Use が, not を: 料理が上手です.
大好き (だいすき) = really like, love.
好きじゃありません (don't like) sounds softer than きらいです.

reading.title: わたしのかぞく — My family
reading.text: 私[わたし]はアンナです。大阪[おおさか]に住[す]んでいます。私[わたし]は五人[ごにん]家族[かぞく]です。父[ちち]と母[はは]と兄[あに]と妹[いもうと]がいます。父[ちち]は警察官[けいさつかん]で、とてもまじめです。母[はは]は看護師[かんごし]です。明[あか]るくて、料理[りょうり]が上手[じょうず]です。兄[あに]は二十五歳[にじゅうごさい]で、もう結婚[けっこん]しています。今[いま]は東京[とうきょう]に住[す]んでいます。妹[いもうと]はまだ高校生[こうこうせい]です。スポーツが大好[だいす]きですが、勉強[べんきょう]はきらいです。私[わたし]の趣味[しゅみ]は音楽[おんがく]です。ピアノが好[す]きですが、まだ下手[へた]です。
reading.en: I'm Anna. I live in Osaka. There are five people in my family: my father, my mother, my older brother, my younger sister and me. My father is a police officer, and he is very serious. My mother is a nurse. She is cheerful and good at cooking. My older brother is twenty-five and already married. He lives in Tokyo now. My younger sister is still a high school student. She loves sports, but she doesn't like studying. My hobby is music. I like the piano, but I'm still not good at it.
